blocks.text: A 52-year-old woman wakes with the room spinning violently. Her eyes jerk rhythmically to one side, she vomits, and she cannot stand. Her hearing is normal. Something in the inner ear has suddenly told the brain that her head is rotating, even though she is lying still.

blocks.markdown:
**Sound transduction.** Sound is a pressure wave. The pinna and external acoustic meatus collect it, and it vibrates the **tympanic membrane**. The vibration passes through the three **ossicles** of the middle ear, **malleus, incus and stapes**, to the **oval window** of the cochlea. The middle ear acts as an **impedance matcher**: the large tympanic membrane concentrates force onto the much smaller stapes footplate, so pressure is amplified, because pressure equals force divided by area. The ossicular lever adds a smaller gain. Without this, most airborne sound would be reflected at the air-fluid boundary.

The stapes moves the **perilymph** of the **scala vestibuli**. The wave deflects the **basilar membrane**, setting up a travelling wave whose peak position depends on frequency: **high frequencies peak near the base** (narrow, stiff), **low frequencies near the apex** (wide, floppy). This is **tonotopy**.

blocks.caption: Pressure gain from the area ratio of the tympanic membrane to the oval window (the lever action of the ossicles adds a smaller factor).

blocks.markdown: On the basilar membrane sits the **organ of Corti**, containing **inner hair cells** (the main sensory transducers, synapsing on type I spiral ganglion neurones) and **outer hair cells** (amplifiers). Hair cell **stereocilia** project into **endolymph**, which is unusual because it is high in $\text{K}^+$ and has a positive potential (the endocochlear potential). When the basilar membrane moves, stereocilia are deflected against the **tectorial membrane**; this opens mechanically-gated channels, and $\text{K}^+$ flows in from the endolymph, **depolarising** the hair cell. Voltage-gated $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels open and the cell releases **glutamate** onto the afferent terminals. Signals pass via spiral ganglion cells in the **cochlear nerve** (part of the vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII) to the cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body and primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

blocks.title: Pressure gain across the middle ear
blocks.prompt: A model middle ear has an effective tympanic membrane area of 50 mm$^2$ and a stapes footplate area of 3.2 mm$^2$. Estimate the pressure gain from area ratio alone.

steps.text: Pressure = force / area. The same force collected over the tympanic membrane is delivered to the footplate.
So pressure at the footplate / pressure at the membrane = $A_{TM}/A_{oval}$.
The lever action of the ossicles adds a further small gain, which is ignored here.

blocks.answer: About 16-fold (approximately 15.6) from area ratio alone, which compensates for the loss at the air-fluid interface.

blocks.title: Conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
blocks.text: Conductive hearing loss is a failure to transmit sound through the external or middle ear (wax, perforation, effusion, otosclerosis). Sensorineural hearing loss is a failure of the cochlea, cochlear nerve or central auditory pathway (hair cell loss, ageing, noise, acoustic neuroma).

blocks.markdown: **Rinne and Weber tests** use a 512 Hz tuning fork. In the **Rinne test** the vibrating fork is held first against the mastoid (bone conduction, BC) and then in front of the ear (air conduction, AC). Normally **AC is louder than BC** (Rinne positive). In conductive loss BC is louder (**Rinne negative**). In the **Weber test** the fork is placed on the midline of the forehead and the patient says in which ear it is louder: normally it is heard centrally. In **conductive loss it lateralises to the affected (worse) ear**. In **sensorineural loss it lateralises to the better ear**.

blocks.caption: The two tests are used together.

blocks.title: Interpreting tuning fork tests
blocks.prompt: In a patient with right-sided hearing loss, the Rinne test is negative on the right and positive on the left. The Weber test is heard louder in the right ear. What is the diagnosis?

steps.text: Rinne negative on the right means bone conduction exceeds air conduction there, which implies a conductive problem in the right ear.
Weber lateralising to the right fits a conductive loss in the right ear, because conductive loss lateralises toward the affected side.
The left Rinne is positive, so the left ear is normal.

blocks.answer: Right conductive hearing loss. A sensorineural right loss would instead give a positive Rinne and Weber toward the left.

blocks.markdown:
**The vestibular system.** The **semicircular canals** detect angular acceleration and the **utricle and saccule** detect linear acceleration and gravity. Hair cells in the canal ampullae are deflected by endolymph inertia during head rotation. Each vestibular nerve fires tonically at rest; head rotation raises firing on the side toward which the head turns and lowers it on the other. The brain compares left and right.

The **vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)** keeps the image steady on the retina during head movement. Signals pass through the vestibular nuclei to the nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV and VI, moving the eyes **equal and opposite** to the head. **VOR gain** is eye velocity divided by head velocity, normally about 1. **Nystagmus** is a rhythmic eye movement with a **slow phase** (vestibular drift) and a **fast corrective phase**, and it is named for the fast phase. If one labyrinth stops firing, the brain interprets the imbalance as rotation away from the lesion: the slow phase drifts toward the damaged side and the fast phase beats away from it.

blocks.title: Turning the head to the left
blocks.prompt: Describe the VOR and nystagmus when a seated person's head is turned to the left.

steps.text: The left horizontal canal is excited and the right inhibited, so the left vestibular nerve fires faster.
Through the vestibular and ocular motor nuclei, the eyes are driven slowly to the right, equal and opposite, keeping gaze fixed.
When the eyes reach the limit of their range, a fast saccade resets them to the left, producing the fast phase of nystagmus.

blocks.answer: Slow phase to the right (vestibular), fast phase to the left (corrective); the nystagmus is described as left-beating.

blocks.title: Name nystagmus by its fast phase
blocks.text: Nystagmus is named for the fast phase, but the slow phase is the vestibular signal. A peripheral vestibular lesion produces nystagmus that beats away from the damaged side.

points: Sound passes through the tympanic membrane, malleus, incus and stapes to the oval window; the area ratio amplifies pressure.
Basilar membrane vibration deflects hair cell stereocilia, K+ enters from endolymph, hair cells depolarise and release glutamate onto cochlear nerve fibres.
Rinne and Weber tests distinguish conductive (Rinne negative, Weber toward the affected ear) from sensorineural loss (Rinne positive, Weber toward the better ear).
The VOR moves the eyes opposite to the head; nystagmus has a slow vestibular phase and a fast corrective phase and beats away from a lesioned labyrinth.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the middle ear ossicles from the tympanic membrane to the oval window?

distractorRationale.b: The malleus attaches to the tympanic membrane first.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the malleus contacts the tympanic membrane and the stapes footplate sits in the oval window.
distractorRationale.d: The stapes is the last ossicle.

questions.explanation: Vibration passes from the tympanic membrane to the malleus, then the incus, then the stapes, whose footplate drives the oval window.

questions.stem: In a patient, the effective area of the tympanic membrane is 45 mm^2 and the area of the stapes footplate is 3.0 mm^2. Using the area ratio alone, what is the pressure gain (dimensionless)?
questions.explanation: The same force is applied over a smaller area, so pressure rises by the area ratio: 45 / 3.0 = 15. This amplification helps overcome the impedance mismatch between air and cochlear fluid.

questions.stem: What is the principal event that depolarises a cochlear inner hair cell when its stereocilia are deflected?

options.text: K+ entry from endolymph through mechanically gated channels
Cl- efflux from the hair cell
Ca2+ release from the tectorial membrane

questions.correctOptionText: K+ entry from endolymph through mechanically gated channels

distractorRationale.a: Perilymph is rich in Na+, but the stereocilia are bathed in endolymph.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: endolymph is high in K+ and positive, so K+ enters and depolarises.
distractorRationale.c: Cl- efflux is not the transduction mechanism.
distractorRationale.d: The tectorial membrane is an extracellular structure.

questions.explanation: Stereocilia deflection opens mechanically gated channels, and K+ flows in from the K+-rich endolymph. The resulting depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and triggers glutamate release.

questions.stem: Where along the basilar membrane is the maximum response to a high-frequency tone?

options.text: Near the base, close to the oval window

questions.correctOptionText: Near the base, close to the oval window

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the base is narrow and stiff and tuned to high frequencies.
distractorRationale.b: The apex is wide and floppy, tuned to low frequencies.
distractorRationale.d: The response is tonotopically organised, not uniform.

questions.explanation: The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base and wide and compliant at the apex, so high frequencies peak at the base and low frequencies at the apex.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with reduced hearing has a Rinne test that is positive in both ears, and a Weber test that lateralises to his right ear. Which interpretation is most consistent?

distractorRationale.a: Conductive loss would give a negative Rinne in the right ear.
distractorRationale.b: A left conductive loss would give a negative Rinne on the left and Weber toward the left.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: positive Rinne indicates a sensorineural pattern; Weber to the better (right) ear implies the left cochlea or nerve is affected.
distractorRationale.d: Right sensorineural loss would lateralise Weber to the left.

questions.explanation: A positive Rinne with reduced hearing indicates sensorineural loss. In sensorineural loss the Weber lateralises to the healthier ear, so a right-sided Weber places the lesion on the left.

questions.stem: True or false: in sensorineural hearing loss, air conduction remains better than bone conduction (Rinne positive).
questions.explanation: In sensorineural loss the middle ear conducts normally, so air conduction still exceeds bone conduction, although both are reduced. Only a conductive loss reverses this pattern.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a blocked left ear canal after wax impaction. Predict the results of the Rinne test (left ear) and Weber test, and explain what type of hearing loss this represents.
markingGuide: Conductive hearing loss in the left ear
Rinne in the left ear is negative: bone conduction is better than air conduction
Weber lateralises to the left (affected) ear
Bone conduction bypasses the blocked canal and middle ear; cochlea is normal
Mention that ambient noise masking is reduced in the blocked ear, so the Weber sounds louder there (or that bone conduction stimulates the cochlea directly)
questions.explanation: A blocked canal reduces air-conducted sound but leaves the cochlea and bone conduction normal, so BC exceeds AC (Rinne negative). The Weber lateralises toward the blocked ear because bone-conducted sound is relatively unmasked there.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the vestibulo-ocular reflex?

options.text: To constrict the pupil in bright light
To move the eyes equal and opposite to head movement and keep the image stable on the retina
To focus the lens for near vision
To convert sound into eye movements

questions.correctOptionText: To move the eyes equal and opposite to head movement and keep the image stable on the retina

distractorRationale.a: That is the pupillary light reflex.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: this is the VOR, which stabilises gaze.
distractorRationale.d: The VOR is not driven by sound.

questions.explanation: During head rotation the VOR drives eye movement of equal speed in the opposite direction, so the image stays fixed on the fovea. Vestibular signals pass via the vestibular nuclei to the extraocular motor nuclei.

questions.stem: During a head impulse test, the head is turned at 150 degrees per second and the eyes move in the opposite direction at 120 degrees per second. VOR gain is eye velocity divided by head velocity. What is the gain (dimensionless)?
questions.explanation: Gain = 120 / 150 = 0.8. A normal gain is about 1, so 0.8 indicates under-compensation and the eyes slip off the target, as seen with a hypofunctioning vestibular system.

questions.stem: A patient has acute loss of function of the left vestibular nerve. Which description of the resulting spontaneous peripheral nystagmus is correct?

options.text: Slow phase to the left, fast phase to the right
Slow phase to the right, fast phase to the left
No nystagmus because the VOR is bilateral

questions.correctOptionText: Slow phase to the left, fast phase to the right

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the right side dominates, imitating a rightward head turn so the slow phase drifts to the left; the fast phase beats away from the lesion.
distractorRationale.b: This would be seen with a right-sided lesion.
distractorRationale.c: Nystagmus has opposite slow and fast phases.
distractorRationale.d: Unilateral loss creates an imbalance that does cause nystagmus.

questions.explanation: With the left side silent, the brainstem sees dominant right-sided input, as if the head were turning right, and drives the eyes slowly to the left. A fast corrective saccade then beats to the right, so nystagmus beats away from the lesion.
